# R0 Prefaces + Introduction — Moo Galatians BECNT
**Range:** raw lines 168–223 + 880–1869
**Lines actually read:** L168–L223 (prefaces) and L880–L1869 (Introduction through outline) as present in cache
**Claim count:** 46

## Claims

### C-R0-001
- **topic_tags:** [moo-galatians-becnt, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo (via series editors Yarbrough/Stein) frames BECNT as informed evangelical commentary blending scholarly depth with readability, aimed especially at pastors and expositors of Scripture as the uniquely inspired Word of God.
- **quote:** "The chief concern of the Baker Exegetical Commentary on the New Testament (BECNT) is to provide, within the framework of informed evangelical thought, commentaries that blend scholarly depth with readability"
- **locus:** L170
- **passage:** Series Preface

### C-R0-002
- **topic_tags:** [moo-galatians-becnt, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Series contributors share belief in Scripture’s trustworthiness and essential unity and treat historic creeds and many Reformation documents as arising from a legitimate reading of Scripture, providing a proper interpretive framework.
- **quote:** "the contributors share a belief in the trustworthiness and essential unity of Scripture. They also consider that the historic formulations of Christian doctrine, such as the ecumenical creeds and many of the documents originating in the sixteenth-century Reformation, arose from a legitimate reading of Scripture"
- **locus:** L178
- **passage:** Series Preface

### C-R0-003
- **topic_tags:** [douglas-moo, moo-galatians-becnt]
- **claim:** Moo regularly cites only nine Galatians commentaries for their exegetical excellence and/or distinctive views: Lightfoot, Burton, Betz, Bruce, Mussner, Longenecker, Dunn, Martyn, and de Boer.
- **quote:** "I have therefore chosen to cite regularly only a handful of commentaries… written by J. B. Lightfoot, Ernest deWitt Burton, Hans Dieter Betz, F. F. Bruce, Franz Mussner, Richard Longenecker, James Dunn, Louis Martyn, and Martinus de Boer."
- **locus:** L214
- **passage:** Author’s Note to the Reader

### C-R0-004
- **topic_tags:** [douglas-moo, moo-galatians-becnt]
- **claim:** Moo’s own Galatians translations aim to reflect Greek form for commentary purposes and are not good translations; other Scripture citations are from NIV 2011 unless noted.
- **quote:** "the translations of Galatians… are my own. They are attempts to reflect in English as much of the form of the underlying Greek as possible… they are far from being good translations of the Greek"
- **locus:** L218
- **passage:** Author’s Note to the Reader

### C-R0-005
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, paul-apostle, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo states that the letter identifies its author as “Paul the Apostle” (1:1), is full of corroborating personal references, and that from earliest days Paul’s authorship has been acknowledged and never seriously challenged.
- **quote:** "The author of the Letter to the Galatians identifies himself as “Paul the Apostle” (1:1)… From the earliest days of the church, Paul’s authorship of Galatians has been acknowledged and never seriously challenged."
- **locus:** L884–L886
- **passage:** Author

### C-R0-006
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, paul-apostle, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo holds that Gal 6:11 (“large letters… with my own hand”) probably applies only to 6:11 and following, not the whole letter; if an amanuensis wrote the bulk, the letter’s strongly personal nature argues for near word-for-word dictation rather than free composition by a confidant.
- **quote:** "If Paul used an amanuensis in writing the bulk of Galatians (which is probable), the strongly personal nature of the letter argues for a situation closer to word-for-word dictation."
- **locus:** L886
- **passage:** Author / amanuensis

### C-R0-007
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, circumcision, justification, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo’s occasion summary: omitting thanksgiving, Paul decries flirtation with “another gospel” propagated by false teachers who insist Gentile faith in Christ be supplemented by circumcision and other Mosaic-law elements (esp. 5:2–4).
- **quote:** "This counterfeit gospel is being propagated by false teachers who are “confusing” the Gentile Galatians (1:7; 5:10) by insisting that their faith in Christ be supplemented by submission to circumcision and other elements of the Mosaic law (esp. 5:2–4)."
- **locus:** L890
- **passage:** Occasion for the Letter

### C-R0-008
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo structures Paul’s response in three stages: (1) Paul’s experience and the law / Jerusalem apostles (1:11–2:21); (2) Galatians’ experience and Scripture—justification and Abraham’s seed by faith apart from torah (3:1–5:12); (3) conduct by faith and Spirit apart from torah (5:13–6:18).
- **quote:** "Paul responds to this challenge in three stages. First, he uses his own experience… Second, he uses the Galatians’ own experience and especially Scripture… Third, he shows that conduct pleasing to God is secured by that same faith and the work of God’s Spirit apart from torah"
- **locus:** L890
- **passage:** Occasion for the Letter

### C-R0-009
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo notes “Galatia” in Paul’s day had both an ethnic/geographical (Celtic people in north-central Anatolia) and a political/geographical (Roman province including south) referent.
- **quote:** "In Paul’s day, then, “Galatia” had both an ethnic/geographical and a political/geographical referent."
- **locus:** L898
- **passage:** Destination and Date

### C-R0-010
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo treats the South Galatian theory as destination to churches of Acts 13–14 (Pisidian Antioch, Lystra, Iconium, Derbe); it allows a date as early as ~AD 48 before the Jerusalem Council, popularized by Ramsay and Bruce, but does not lock one into an early date.
- **quote:** "Because the churches of the first missionary journey are located in the southern part of provincial Galatia, this view… has become known as the “South Galatian” theory… It should be stressed, however, that a South Galatian destination does not lock us into an early date"
- **locus:** L906
- **passage:** Destination options

### C-R0-011
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo describes the classic North Galatian theory (Lightfoot; still widely held, esp. by German scholars) as Paul writing to ethnic Galatia (Ancyra, Pessinus, Tavium) sometime on the third missionary journey (~AD 55–56).
- **quote:** "the classic “North Galatian” theory holds that Paul wrote to ethnic Galatia, with its key cities Ancyra, Pessinus, and Tavium, sometime during the third missionary journey (perhaps around AD 55–56)."
- **locus:** L908
- **passage:** Destination options

### C-R0-012
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo judges the lexical argument about “Galatia/Galatians” inconclusive: the terms could refer either to the Roman province and its residents or to the ethnic region and its people.
- **quote:** "The argument about the terms “Galatia” and “Galatians” is therefore inconclusive: they could refer either to the Roman province and people living in that province or to an ethnic region and to the people living in that region."
- **locus:** L918
- **passage:** Destination

### C-R0-013
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo slightly prefers a South Galatian reading of Acts 16:6 / 18:23 but finds the evidence too finely balanced for high probability; yet probable movements of Paul slightly favor a South Galatian destination.
- **quote:** "We slightly prefer the South Galatian reading; but the evidence is too finely balanced to justify any great degree of probability… the probable movements of Paul and his companions slightly favor a South Galatian destination of the letter."
- **locus:** L928–L930
- **passage:** Destination / Paul’s travels

### C-R0-014
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Supporting South Galatia, Moo notes: North Galatia was not very Romanized; major Roman roads there only in the 70s–80s; evidence for a Pauline mission in North Galatia is uncertain, while South Galatia is explicit and unquestioned.
- **quote:** "evidence for a Pauline mission in South Galatia is explicit and unquestioned; evidence for such a mission in North Galatia is uncertain."
- **locus:** L928
- **passage:** Destination / Paul’s travels

### C-R0-015
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, douglas-moo, acts-paul-tensions]
- **claim:** Moo assumes Acts’ historical accuracy in reconstructing chronology (while noting scholars who dismiss Luke); most who use Acts identify Gal 1:18–19 with Acts 9:26–29, but Gal 2:1–10 is debated as either Acts 15 (Apostolic Council) or Acts 11:27–30 (famine-relief visit).
- **quote:** "Is Paul describing the same meeting that Luke depicts in Acts 15…? Or is Paul describing an earlier Jerusalem meeting, perhaps one that took place during the so-called famine relief visit… Acts 11:27–30"
- **locus:** L1156–L1158
- **passage:** Date / Gal 1–2 and Acts

### C-R0-016
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, douglas-moo, acts-paul-tensions]
- **claim:** Moo holds chronological notices (three years; fourteen years) do not settle Gal 2 = Acts 11 vs 15 because of dating imprecision, whether fourteen years runs from conversion or first visit, and inclusive vs exclusive counting.
- **quote:** "these notices do not help much because of three significant variables. First, we cannot date the key events… Second, we cannot be sure whether the “fourteen years” of 2:1 are to be counted from Paul’s conversion or from his first Jerusalem visit. And third, we cannot know whether “three years” and “fourteen years” are to be counted inclusively… or exclusively"
- **locus:** L1160
- **passage:** Chronological considerations

### C-R0-017
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, douglas-moo, acts-paul-tensions]
- **claim:** Because Moo reads Gal 2:2 as relatively clear that the meeting was private, he inclines very weakly to locate Gal 2:1–10 during the famine-relief visit (Acts 11:27–30) rather than the public Council of Acts 15.
- **quote:** "Because we think that 2:2 is relatively clear about the private nature of the meeting, we incline very weakly to locate the meeting of Gal. 2:1–10 during the famine-relief visit of Paul to Jerusalem (Acts 11:27–30)."
- **locus:** L1318
- **passage:** Parallels Gal 2 / Acts 11 / 15

### C-R0-018
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, douglas-moo, acts-paul-tensions]
- **claim:** Moo finds considerable merit in two arguments from silence for a pre-Council date: (1) if Gal 2 = Acts 15, Paul would have omitted Acts 11 yet still seems to detail all contacts with the pillars; (2) failure to mention the Jerusalem decree on circumcision is hard to explain if the Council had already met.
- **quote:** "These two arguments, combined with the probability that the meeting of Gal. 2 was a private one, lead us to align Gal. 2:1–10 with Acts 11:27–30. Paul’s failure to mention the Apostolic Council visit to Jerusalem can only be explained, then, if he wrote before the Council had met."
- **locus:** L1328
- **passage:** Arguments from silence / date

### C-R0-019
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, douglas-moo, acts-paul-tensions]
- **claim:** Moo’s preferred scenario sequence: plant (and follow-up) South Galatian churches → return to Antioch → agitators arrive in South Galatia during that stay → writing of Galatians → Jerusalem Council.
- **quote:** "Planting (and follow-up visit) of the churches in South Galatia… Return to Antioch… Arrival of agitators in the South Galatian churches… Writing of Galatians… Jerusalem Council (Acts 15:1–29)"
- **locus:** L1330–L1338
- **passage:** Sequence if pre-Council

### C-R0-020
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, douglas-moo, justification]
- **claim:** Against dating Galatians with Romans from shared vocabulary/themes (law, righteousness, Abraham, adoption, crucified-with, love-command, Spirit), Moo argues similarities reflect similar occasions more than a developmental trajectory; Galatians was probably written AD 48 just before the Apostolic Conference and is Paul’s earliest extant letter.
- **quote:** "Galatians, we conclude, was probably written in AD 48 just before the Apostolic Conference of Acts 15. It is the earliest extant letter of Paul."
- **locus:** L1358–L1360
- **passage:** Date conclusion

### C-R0-021
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, circumcision, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo: Paul writes to combat people pressuring Galatians to undergo circumcision and submit to Mosaic law as a means of completing Christian experience; Jewish liturgical calendar is hinted in “days and months and seasons and years” (4:9–10); climax at 5:1–6.
- **quote:** "Paul writes Galatians to combat people who are pressuring the Galatians to undergo circumcision and submit to the law of Moses as a means of completing their Christian experience."

- **passage:** Occasion and Purpose

### C-R0-022
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo rejects a two-front war (legalism 1:1–5:12 vs antinomians 5:13–6:10); a single Christian-Jewish opposition adequately explains the ethical section’s relation to the theological part.
- **quote:** "this interpretation of the situation Paul addresses introduces an unnecessary complication that is not required by the argument of the letter. The relationship of the so-called ethical part of the letter (5:13–6:10) to its “theological” part (1:1–5:12) is adequately explained on the hypothesis of a single Christian-Jewish opposition"
- **locus:** L1370

### C-R0-023
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, covenantal-nomism, new-perspective-on-paul, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo largely agrees with Dunn that agitators focused on a “second phase” of Christian experience (Sanders’s “staying in” not “getting in”), but suggests the focus was not only/mainly “staying in” but ultimate vindication in the judgment.
- **quote:** "We think this general reading of the letter is very much on target… We would, however, suggest that the focus was not only, or perhaps even mainly, on “staying in” but on ultimate vindication in the judgment"
- **locus:** L1372
- **passage:** Agitators / “complete”

### C-R0-024
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, douglas-moo, peter-apostle, james-the-just]
- **claim:** Moo (following Jewett) links agitators’ avoidance of persecution for the cross (6:12) to concern not to offend fellow Jews amid rising Zealot influence; similar motivation may lie behind “men from James” at Antioch (2:11–14).
- **quote:** "Paul’s claim that the agitators were acting in order to avoid being persecuted for the cross of Christ (6:12) may best be explained if they were concerned to avoid giving offense to fellow Jews… The same motivation may lie behind the “men from James” who stirred up so much trouble at Antioch (2:11–14)."
- **locus:** L1374
- **passage:** Agitators’ motivation

### C-R0-025
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo holds agitators claimed a Jerusalem connection (Paul’s focus on Jerusalem relations; Hagar allegory and “present city of Jerusalem,” 4:25); they were Christian but Paul views their position as fundamentally Jewish in orientation (contra Martyn’s pure rival-missionary portrait).
- **quote:** "Not only, then, did the agitators claim to represent Jerusalem; their perspective is also one that Paul identifies with Judaism in general… Christian they clearly were; but Paul’s argument makes clear that he views their position as fundamentally Jewish in orientation"
- **locus:** L1376
- **passage:** Agitators / Jerusalem

### C-R0-026
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, douglas-moo, hellenized-diaspora-jews]
- **claim:** Moo rejects Mark Nanos’s view that “influencers” were local Jews managing proselyte admission (inner-Jewish argument): fatal is 1:6–9—“another gospel” only makes sense if they claimed to be Christians.
- **quote:** "fatal to it is his unconvincing explanation of 1:6–9. Paul’s assertion in this passage that the agitators were preaching “another gospel” (1:6–9) only makes sense if they were claiming to be Christians"

- **passage:** Agitators / Nanos

### C-R0-027
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, abraham, circumcision, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo reconstructs agitators’ scriptural case: true Abrahamic people identified by circumcision and Mosaic law; as Christians they add Messiah-faith and allow Gentile inclusion, but still require traditional proselyte requirements; likely appeal to Abraham’s faith then circumcision (Gen 15 then 17).
- **quote:** "they also insisted that Gentiles who wanted to join Abraham’s people… needed to add to their faith in Christ those traditional requirements imposed on Gentiles who wanted to convert to Judaism: circumcision and adherence to the law of Moses."
- **locus:** L1382
- **passage:** Logic of Paul’s Response

### C-R0-028
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, new-creation, new-covenant, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** For Moo, Paul’s key is the epochal crucified and resurrected Christ inaugurating eschatological “new creation” (6:15); Mosaic covenant with law is temporary, subordinate to the Abrahamic covenant (3:15–25); many reduce the issue to “What time is it?”
- **quote:** "Central to Paul’s discontinuous reading is the insistence that the Mosaic covenant, with its focus on the law, is a temporary phase in salvation history, subordinate to and intended to accomplish something different than the Abrahamic covenant (3:15–25)."
- **locus:** L1384
- **passage:** Logic / salvation history

### C-R0-029
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, justification, new-perspective-on-paul, covenantal-nomism, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo summarizes traditional reading: antithesis of torah-doing vs Christ-faith reflects a more general human believing vs human doing contrast; after Sanders’s covenantal nomism, NPP (esp. Dunn) instead explains the antithesis via Gentile inclusion and end of the torah era for the people of God.
- **quote:** "According to Dunn, Paul sets faith in Christ and doing the torah against one another because only the former opens the way for full inclusion of Gentiles in the people of God and because the era in which torah observance was required of the people of God ended with the coming of the Messiah."
- **locus:** L1390
- **passage:** Logic vs NPP

### C-R0-030
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, new-perspective-on-paul, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo notes later Dunn affirms both ethnic restrictiveness and “Lutheran” concern about human achievement (both/and); Barclay objects to having one’s historical cake and eating it theologically, resisting extrapolation of the Christ-torah antithesis to broader principles, and instead grounds the ban on torah in Christ as “unconditioned gift” that subverts standards of worth.
- **quote:** "Barclay concludes, then, that grace is indeed central to the logic of Galatians, but not in the way the Reformers thought. Paul is not arguing from “a general principle that rules out ‘law’ or ‘work’ as elements of soteriology,” but from a recognition that “the unconditioned Christ-gift . . . subverts and reconstitutes what counts as worth”"
- **locus:** L1392
- **passage:** Logic / Barclay

### C-R0-031
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, justification, new-perspective-on-paul, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo’s own stance: traditional but currently unfashionable—underlying Paul’s polemic against doing torah is concern about human “doing” in general; sinful humans cannot render the obedience God deserves; works of the law, like any human work, fall short, leaving incorporation into Christ by faith as the only means of righteousness (line back at least to Chrysostom).
- **quote:** "we argue for the traditional but currently unfashionable view that underlying Paul’s polemic against doing the torah in Galatians is his concern about human “doing” in general. The problem with human doing is that it is always and necessarily inadequate"
- **locus:** L1398
- **passage:** Logic of Galatians — Moo’s position

### C-R0-032
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, justification, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo’s three elements validating move from particular “works of the law” to universal “works”: (1) verb “doing” (ποιέω) at critical points (3:10, 12; 5:3); (2) assumed inability to do all the law in 3:10 (and 5:3); (3) “grace” language (esp. 2:21; 5:4) implying rejection of human achievement.
- **quote:** "Three elements in Paul’s argument show that it is, indeed, valid to move from the particular phrase “works of the law” to the universal issue of “works.”"
- **locus:** L1400
- **passage:** Works of the law → works

### C-R0-033
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, justification, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo’s syllogism for Gal 3:10: only those who do everything written in the law escape the curse; no one can do everything written in the law (assumed); therefore no one who depends on doing the law escapes the curse.
- **quote:** "Only those who do everything written in the law will escape the curse (Gal. 3:10b). No one can do everything written in the law (assumed). Therefore, no one who depends on doing the law will escape the curse (v. 10a)."
- **locus:** L1406–L1410
- **passage:** Gal 3:10 logic

### C-R0-034
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, justification, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Against the objection that Judaism thought the law doable via atonement, Moo prefers: after Christ, OT sacrificial atonement is null; only two options remain—justification in Christ by faith, or through the law now requiring “all” without sacrifice.
- **quote:** "In the time after Christ, then, one is faced with two, and only two, options: find justification in Christ by faith; or find justification through the law, a justification that can now, apart from the provision of sacrifice, be secured only by doing “all” the law"
- **locus:** L1418
- **passage:** Inability and sacrifice

### C-R0-035
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, justification, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Citing Westerholm, Moo: fundamental question is not what is wrong with Judaism/Sinaitic law but what is wrong with humanity that Judaism and the law cannot remedy; distinction between human doing and believing, while not the focus, underlies Galatians.
- **quote:** "“The fundamental question addressed by Galatians thus is not ‘What is wrong with Judaism (or the Sinaitic law)?’ but ‘What is wrong with humanity that Judaism (and the Sinaitic law) cannot remedy?’”"
- **locus:** L1426
- **passage:** Pessimistic anthropology

### C-R0-036
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, new-creation, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo affirms apocalyptic categories (rescue from present evil age; new creation; apocalypse of Jesus Christ) emphasized by Martyn, but rejects Martyn’s denial of real salvation history: law remains God’s law; Christ is climax of an unfolding story—salvation history and apocalyptic need not be opposed.
- **quote:** "Salvation history and apocalyptic, in other words, need not be set in opposition: Christ… can only be fully understood as the climax (apocalyptic) of an unfolding story (salvation history)."
- **locus:** L1436
- **passage:** Salvation History and Apocalyptic

### C-R0-037
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo judges “gospel” the best single unifying theme: language dense in chs. 1–2; “truth of the gospel” (2:5, 14); 2:15–21 as summary of that truth; good news of apocalypse of Jesus Christ, death for sinners, new creation, and above all justification by grace and faith alone.
- **quote:** "a good case can be made for identifying the gospel as the best single unifying theme of the letter… above all, justification by grace and by faith alone (2:15–21)—this gospel is the bedrock on which Paul builds his argument"
- **locus:** L1440
- **passage:** The Gospel

### C-R0-038
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, douglas-moo, justification]
- **claim:** For Moo, incorporation into Christ is a fundamental theological center: blessing promised “in” Abraham given to those who belong to Christ the singular seed; both justification and sanctification via union with Christ—the “double gift” Calvin emphasizes.
- **quote:** "Incorporation into Christ is a fundamental theological concept in the letter… Those who are “in Christ” enjoy the “blessing of Abraham,” in the context of justification (3:14); and “those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh”… Thus both justification and sanctification are given believers via their union with Christ"
- **locus:** L1446
- **passage:** Christ / incorporation

### C-R0-039
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, holy-spirit, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo: Spirit marks inauguration of Christian experience (3:2, 5; 4:6) and must continue as means of finishing (3:3; 5:5); in 5:13–6:10 Spirit leads and produces fruit, but believers must walk/keep in step with the Spirit; “promise of the Spirit” (3:14) fulfills OT prophecies of Spirit-enabled obedience.
- **quote:** "the Spirit must also become the means by which believers continue and complete their Christian experience: “After beginning by means of the Spirit, are you now trying to finish by means of the flesh?” (3:3)."
- **locus:** L1450
- **passage:** The Spirit

### C-R0-040
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, douglas-moo, stoicheia]
- **claim:** Moo on law: almost always torah; temporary supervisor until the seed; cannot give life; brings curse because of inability (3:10; 5:3); “under the law” means under the law’s authority (not primarily “under the curse”); “law of Christ” (6:2) is ethical guidance of the new covenant, not OT law as fulfilled in Christ; fulfilling the law (5:14) via love command.
- **quote:** "we think a more natural reading of the phrase… is to view it as contrasting “the law of Moses” with “the law of Christ.” The phrase is a succinct way of summarizing the ethical guidance given to new covenant believers, found in Christ’s teaching and the teaching of his accredited apostles"
- **locus:** L1474–L1476

### C-R0-041
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, pistis-christou, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo rejects subjective-genitive “faith/faithfulness of Christ” for πίστις Χριστοῦ (despite its recent popularity after Hays); concludes traditional objective “faith in Christ” is well grounded by parallel constructions and Galatians context; faith is the human-side corollary of grace—by faith alone is the key theological argument.
- **quote:** "We conclude, then, that the traditional interpretation of the phrase πίστις Χριστοῦ as a reference to human believing “in” Christ is well grounded… The indispensability of and exclusivity of faith—not only “by faith,” but also “by faith alone”—is the key theological argument of the letter."
- **locus:** L1648
- **passage:** “The Faith of Christ”

### C-R0-042
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, justification, new-perspective-on-paul, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Against N. T. Wright’s redefinition of justification as primarily membership in God’s people / table-fellowship status, Moo insists justify retains forensic “declare righteous”; membership and justification are closely related but not identical; content of justification by faith should be distinguished from its scope (Gathercole).
- **quote:** "There is no good contextual reason to insist that “justify” in 2:16 must be redefined to mean, or to include, the notion of membership in God’s people… “The content of the doctrine of justification by faith should be distinguished from its scope.”"
- **locus:** L1688
- **passage:** Justification / Wright

### C-R0-043
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, justification, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo rejects folding transformative ethics into justification: in Galatians δικ- language is forensic (status before God); union with Christ produces both forensic justification and Spirit-wrought transformation as inseparable but distinguishable benefits; union with Christ, not justification, lies at the heart of Paul’s theology, yet forensic justification is a primary benefit.
- **quote:** "Union with Christ, not justification, lies at the heart of Paul’s theology. But forensic justification is one of the primary and critical benefits that people who belong to Christ by faith receive."
- **locus:** L1694
- **passage:** Justification / transformation

### C-R0-044
- **topic_tags:** [galatians, justification, douglas-moo]
- **claim:** Moo on time of justification in Galatians: most references timeless/undetermined or future; letter emphasizes maintaining righteous status and especially final vindication at judgment (not mainly “how you get saved” / initial justification, though initial is presumed); Galatians is about ultimate justification.

## Coverage summary

This range covers the full Series Preface (BECNT aims, evangelical commitments, format notes), Author’s Preface (Wheaton students, NIV 2011 delay, dedication to Jenny), and Note to the Reader (nine core commentaries; English translations as exegetical tradition; Moo’s formal Greek-reflecting renderings + NIV 2011 elsewhere).

The Introduction treats: authorship (uncontested Paul; probable amanuensis with near-dictation); occasion (three-stage response to circumcision/law-supplementing “other gospel”); destination (North vs South; lexical inconclusiveness; slight South preference from itinerary/Romanization/Acts evidence); date (Gal 2 weakly = Acts 11; silences favor pre-Council AD 48 as earliest Paul letter; Romans parallels not decisive for late date); agitators (single Christian-Jewish group; complete/vindication focus; Jerusalem claim; Zealot/persecution motive; reject Nanos and two-front war); logic of response (salvation-historical “what time is it?” plus traditional anthropology of inability and grace vs human doing—against pure NPP/Barclay-Watson particularism); themes (salvation history + apocalyptic held together; gospel as unifying theme; Christ/cross/incorporation; Spirit; law and law of Christ; Christian life 5:13–6:10 as integral); extended treatments of πίστις Χριστοῦ (objective/human faith) and justification/righteousness (OT background; forensic status; against Wright membership-collapse and transformative-justification merges; ultimate/future-leaning vindication); genre/rhetoric (limited value of full rhetorical classification); full outline.

**Gaps / surprises:** No substantial treatment of Marcionites, Pharisees as named historical groups, or James–Paul justification controversy as a named inter-canonical dispute (James is only the Jerusalem figure). Titulus “three-level logic” is not Moo’s label in this range; the multi-level structure is present as salvation-historical + anthropological + grace/faith logic. Ebook duplication not observed in this slice (aside from outline repeated in summary form at L1858–L1866 after the full outline). Cache omits continuous lines between L223 and L880 by design (front matter jump to Introduction).
